In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Fis effect on transposition in the repressor‐on state is mediated by the IAS and is dependent on the presence of a functional repressor, whereas the IAS has an enhancing function on transposition in repressor‐off cells.
Fis is involved in a negative regulatory pathway, which leads to a lower level of the Mu repressor and thereby to a higher frequency of transposition.
Fis can lower Mu transposition frequency by a mechanism which involves the IAS and the repressor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the presence of repressor the level of Fis determines the transposition frequency.
Fis can enhance transposition frequency by increasing the amount of repressor.
Fis can enhance the repressive action of the Mu repressor on transposition by lowering the level of the Mu repressors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the regulation of the Mu transposase is not only determined by the presence of the repressor, but that the repressor can also be modulated by other proteins, in this case Fis.
Fis and Mu repressor can act together to regulate Mu transposition, which may have important consequences for the regulation of other transposable elements.
Fis and repressors can act in concert to inhibit transposition.
